package_info.package_name: Adwind RAT (delivered via malicious JAR dropper)
package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed as JAR via phishing and GitHub Pages)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple variants (e.g., wucgy3jecwgpv.svg, 6da7uj4b4oi2a.pdf, zpmqwjs.docx, hashes: 8ca09bebe64bc1f8a2b5e50d4883f81d58a9f9fc, 981c98fa370ee934a2754a457a830bcf1e381fbe, ce0b09339b565a6613b505a372f83f4003a81190)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is a heavily obfuscated Java-based dropper that delivers the Adwind RAT, a remote access trojan with extensive info-stealing and surveillance capabilities. It employs multiple evasion techniques, persistence mechanisms, and exfiltrates sensitive data to attacker-controlled C&C servers. The malware is distributed via phishing emails containing malicious Office attachments, and leverages disguised file extensions and anti-analysis checks to evade detection.

execution_context.trigger: User opens malicious Office document (XLS/CSV attachment)
execution_context.file_location: BIFF5-format XLS file (External Reference record) or CSV file (Formula injection)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: cmd /c powershell –executionpolicy bypass –W Hidden –command "[download JAR file zpmqwjs.docx]"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the malicious Office document, the code executes a hidden PowerShell command via cmd to download a JAR file from a remote server, writing the file to disk and enabling the next stage of malware execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Office documents should not execute hidden PowerShell commands to download and save executable content from the internet.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Office documents do not trigger shell or PowerShell commands, nor do they download or execute files without explicit user action.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated document processing in enterprise environments may use macros, but never to download JAR files disguised as documents.
key_indicators: Hidden PowerShell execution from Office document
Download of JAR file with misleading extension (e.g., .docx)
Use of legacy BIFF5 format and junk characters for evasion
Formula injection or external reference abuse

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Obfuscated Java code using dynamic invocation and decryption function Gv; locale/language/country checks; public IP and geolocation checks via checkip.amazonaws.com and ipinfo.io.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution of the JAR file, the code decrypts and dynamically invokes functions to check the system's locale, language, and country, then queries external services to determine the public IP and geolocation. If the system is not located in Turkey, the malware proceeds to execute its payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware frequently uses locale and geolocation checks to evade analysis and avoid infecting systems in specific regions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Java applications do not perform anti-analysis checks or restrict execution based on country or language settings.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Region-locked software (e.g., DRM enforcement), but not for evasion or anti-analysis.
key_indicators: Obfuscated Java code with dynamic invocation and decryption routines
Locale, language, and country checks at runtime
External IP and geolocation queries to checkip.amazonaws.com and ipinfo.io
Conditional execution based on geolocation

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After passing evasion checks, the code executes a WMIC command to enumerate installed antivirus products on the system, collects the results, and sends this information to the attacker's C&C server for reconnaissance.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware commonly enumerates security products to tailor attacks, disable defenses, or evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely needs to enumerate antivirus products, especially without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise inventory or asset management tools may query security products, but with user awareness and consent.
key_indicators: WMIC query for antivirus product enumeration
Exfiltration of security product information to remote server
Reconnaissance activity following initial infection

execution_context.trigger: JAR execution (persistence setup after initial payload execution)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the payload is executed, the code writes a registry key under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to point to the malware's path, ensuring the malware is automatically executed on user logon and establishing persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware often abuses registry Run keys to maintain persistence across reboots without user awareness.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers may use Run keys for user-facing applications, but not for hidden or obfuscated payloads.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Auto-starting legitimate applications (e.g., antivirus, cloud sync clients) with user consent.
key_indicators: Registry Run key referencing obfuscated JAR or Java process
Persistence mechanism for non-legitimate or hidden payloads
Registry modification without user notification

execution_context.trigger: JAR execution (payload stage after persistence and evasion)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Adwind RAT core: screenshot capture, webcam/microphone access, file theft, keystroke logging, VPN certificate collection, lateral movement, C&C communication (e.g., connect to 21736.xyz:1505).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After persistence is established, the code enables remote access, captures screenshots, records audio and video from the webcam and microphone, steals files and credentials, logs keystrokes, collects VPN certificates, attempts lateral movement, and communicates with the attacker's C&C server to exfiltrate data and receive commands.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is the core RAT functionality, enabling full compromise, surveillance, and data exfiltration from the victim's system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate Java application should perform all these actions—surveillance, credential theft, and remote control—without explicit user consent and transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support tools may access similar resources, but only with explicit user consent, clear notification, and limited scope.
key_indicators: C&C communication to suspicious domains on non-standard ports
Surveillance capabilities: screenshot, webcam, microphone access
Keystroke logging and credential theft
Lateral movement attempts and VPN certificate collection

execution_context.trigger: JAR execution (post-dropper, file hiding step after persistence setup)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After establishing persistence, the code uses attrib.exe to set the malware file's hidden attribute, making the file invisible in standard Windows Explorer views and reducing the likelihood of user discovery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware frequently hides its files to evade user detection and hinder manual removal.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications rarely hide their executables or core files, especially without user notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System utilities or backup software may hide files for operational reasons, but this is rare and typically documented.
key_indicators: Use of attrib.exe to set hidden attribute on malware files
Obfuscated or misleading file names and extensions
File hiding immediately after persistence setup

attack_chain.action: Phishing email with malicious Office attachment (XLS/CSV) is sent to the victim.
User opens the document, triggering a hidden PowerShell command to download an obfuscated JAR file from a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: JAR file is downloaded and saved to disk.

attack_chain.action: User executes the downloaded JAR file, which performs locale, language, and geolocation checks to evade analysis.
attack_chain.leads_to: If the system is not in Turkey, the malware proceeds to the next stage.

attack_chain.action: JAR file queries installed antivirus products and sends the results to the attacker's C&C server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains reconnaissance on victim's security defenses.

attack_chain.action: JAR writes a registry key for persistence and hides its files using attrib.exe.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware persists across reboots and remains hidden from the user.

attack_chain.action: Adwind RAT payload activates, enabling remote access, surveillance, and data theft.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains full control and exfiltrates data to C&C.

behavioral_signatures: Office document triggers hidden PowerShell or shell commands upon opening
Download and execution of JAR files disguised as documents (e.g., .docx, .svg, .pdf extensions)
Obfuscated Java code with dynamic invocation and runtime decryption routines
Locale, language, and geolocation checks prior to payload execution
WMIC queries for antivirus product enumeration
Registry Run key creation referencing Java/JAR files for persistence
Use of attrib.exe to set hidden attribute on malware files
Outbound C&C communication from Java processes to suspicious domains on non-standard ports
RAT behaviors: screenshot capture, webcam/microphone access, keystroke logging, credential and VPN certificate theft, lateral movement
file_indicators: Office attachments using legacy BIFF5 format with junk characters or formula injection
Downloaded files with document extensions but containing Java bytecode (e.g., .docx, .svg, .pdf)
Registry key: HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run referencing Java/JAR file path
Hidden files named 'Uninstall' or with attractive icons and misleading extensions
network_indicators: Connections to checkip.amazonaws.com and ipinfo.io for geolocation checks
Outbound connections from Java processes to unknown or suspicious domains on non-standard ports
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents that execute PowerShell or shell commands, especially those downloading files with document extensions that contain Java bytecode. Flag downloads of files with mismatched extensions and content. Detect obfuscated Java code with dynamic invocation and anti-analysis checks. Alert on WMIC queries for antivirus products and suspicious registry Run key creation referencing Java/JAR files. Monitor for outbound connections to known C&C domains and non-standard ports from Java processes. Look for RAT behaviors such as screenshot capture, webcam/microphone access, keystroke logging, credential and VPN certificate theft, and lateral movement attempts.
